rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical peak pairs. A moderate gradient duration and temperature provide a useful baseline for subsequent slope and selectivity tests.

All pairs are comfortably resolved, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates how the critical pairs respond to gradient slope.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to recover resolution, while raising temperature to shorten retention and change selectivity within the critical central cluster. This tests whether full resolution can be achieved without a substantial time penalty.

Lower temperature to 50 C while retaining the 12-minute gradient to move away from the near-coelution seen at 60 C. Intermediate temperature may resolve the central cluster while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

At 55 C, interpolation suggests the two temperature-sensitive critical pairs could both approach baseline resolution. Retaining the 12-minute gradient should keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.
Injection 5 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the best method. Test a slightly shallower gradient to assess whether resolution margins can improve while retaining a zero time penalty.
The maximum CRF is already secured. Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention and probe selectivity, while keeping the temperature that resolved the central cluster.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the unresolved pair from injection 7 while preserving its shorter retention. This may provide another maximum-score method with a better minimum-resolution margin.

A further small slope reduction should lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5 while leaving the other central pair resolved. The last peak is projected near 8 minutes, close to the edge of the zero-time-penalty window.

This gradient slope lies between injections 8 and 9, targeting full resolution with the last peak slightly below 8 minutes. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction paired with a shallower gradient improves the critical-pair resolution margins while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes. Previously demonstrated CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmark.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a cooler, faster-gradient alternative for improved resolution margins. Relative to injection 2, changing only temperature isolates whether lower-temperature selectivity resolves the central cluster.

Test an alternative selectivity region where higher starting organic and temperature may carry the near-coeluting central pair through an elution-order reversal. This exploratory run targets a faster fully resolved method; injection 5 already secures the maximum CRF.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover retention and separation of the first two peaks. A steeper gradient tests whether the reversed central pair separates further while maintaining the short analysis time.

Shorten only the gradient duration relative to injection 14 to measure the slope response of its remaining critical pair. This tests the faster, reversed-order separation regime while retaining the established maximum-score methods.

Lower temperature relative to injection 13 to increase retention of the nearly unretained first pair and shift central-cluster selectivity. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic method can achieve full resolution at a shorter analysis time.

Trim injection 5’s unused gradient tail while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and slope. All peaks previously eluted before 8 minutes at this slope, so this method should retain the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a modestly steeper gradient than the maximum-score method to locate the faster edge of its resolution window. The early peaks should remain retained, with the central pair determining whether the time reduction preserves full resolution.

Test an intermediate cooler temperature against injections 2 and 12 to check for a separate full-resolution selectivity window. The last peak should remain below 8 minutes, while the established 55 C methods retain the maximum score.

Use a shallower gradient than injection 16 to test whether both marginal central pairs improve while the first pair remains resolved. The projected last-peak time is near 8 minutes, offering a possible alternative maximum-score method.

Trim the gradient tail of injection 9 while preserving its slope and selectivity, which gave the best minimum resolution among maximum-score runs. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Reduce the slope from injection 11 to test whether its remaining critical pair reaches baseline resolution while preserving the stronger separation of the other central pair. This probes resolution margin around the successful 55 C region, though a small time penalty is possible.

A small slope reduction from injection 22 should raise its critical pair above R = 1.5 while retaining the other pair’s resolution margin. The last peak is projected near 9 minutes, testing whether this improved separation still avoids a time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 9’s gradient to increase separation of its temperature-sensitive central pair while checking that the other critical pair remains above R = 1.5. The last peak should remain below the approximately 9-minute zero-time-penalty boundary.

Use a gradient slope between the maximum-score injections 9 and 24, targeting full resolution with the last peak below 9 minutes. The campaign has already achieved the theoretical maximum CRF of 1.000; this final refinement tests another nearby operating point.
